passage: The residential school in the district town was only forty kilometres from Ramesh's village, but at night it felt like the other side of the world. Lying on the top bunk, he listened for sounds that weren't there: the cow shifting in the shed, Bou's bangles as she scrubbed the vessels, the dog barking at the moon. Instead there were twenty boys breathing and a tap dripping. He thought of the cold rice and curd Bou gave him on summer afternoons, and his throat went tight. Below him, Pintu snored. Ramesh pressed his face into the pillow so nobody would hear. Fourteen was too old to miss your mother. Everyone said so. In the morning, Yamini Didi, the matron, noticed his swollen eyes at the tap and quietly asked him to help her count the laundry.

qa.q: How far was the residential school from Ramesh's village?
qa.a: Only forty kilometres.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh press his face into the pillow?
qa.a: Ramesh was aching for home but feared seeming childish, so the tears stayed hidden from the boys in the dorm.

qa.q: Yamini Didi asked Ramesh to help count laundry. Why might that quiet choice help?
qa.a: It gives Ramesh a private moment with a kind adult, where missing home can be talked about without the others watching.

qa.q: How might Pintu and the other boys be feeling at night?
qa.a: Some of them may be missing home too, even if they also hide it, so Ramesh might not be as alone as it feels.

grounding: A boy at a residential school lies awake missing home sounds and food, hiding tears from dorm-mates.

passage: Abebe had been at the boarding school in Addis Ababa for five weeks. The canteen served pasta on Tuesdays, and every Tuesday he thought of his mother's injera, sour and warm, and the smell of roasting coffee that filled the house in Bahir Dar each Sunday. At night the dorm was quiet except for traffic. No goats, no neighbours calling, no radio from his uncle's shop. He lay awake doing sums in his head so he wouldn't think. At breakfast, his friend Yara said, 'I miss my little brothers so much it hurts.' Abebe laughed and said, 'I don't miss anything. Freedom!' His roommates laughed too. Later, in the library, he opened a photo of the family coffee ceremony and stared at it until the bell rang.

qa.q: What does the canteen serve on Tuesdays?
qa.a: Pasta.

qa.q: Why did Abebe laugh and say "Freedom!" at breakfast?
qa.a: Abebe was missing home badly but didn't want to look childish in front of the roommates, so he covered it with a joke.

qa.q: When Yara admitted missing home, what could Abebe have said instead?
qa.a: Abebe could have quietly agreed and mentioned missing the coffee ceremony; sharing it with one friend might make the nights easier.

qa.q: How might Yara feel when Abebe laughs off missing home?
qa.a: Yara may feel a bit alone or embarrassed after being honest, not knowing that Abebe feels the same.

grounding: A boarding student misses his mother's cooking and home sounds but jokes it away to avoid seeming childish.

passage: Lights-out at the residential school in Pachmarhi was at ten, but Abhinav, thirteen, was still awake at midnight. The dorm smelled of phenyl and damp socks. At home, the pressure cooker would have whistled hours ago, Maa's dal-baati would be finished, and Papa would be locking the gate with the squeak he never oiled. Here there was only a dripping tap and eleven boys breathing. Abhinav pulled the blanket over his head and pressed his lips together hard. From the next bunk, Irfan whispered, "You awake?" Abhinav wiped his face quickly. "Mosquito," he said. "Keeps biting." He didn't want Irfan thinking he was a baby who missed his Maa. He lay still until Irfan's breathing slowed, then played the gate's squeak in his head until he slept.

qa.q: What did the dorm smell of?
qa.a: Phenyl and damp socks.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav blame a mosquito?
qa.a: He was afraid Irfan would think he was childish for missing home and Maa, so he hid his tears.

qa.q: What could help Abhinav with homesickness at the hostel?
qa.a: He could talk to a house parent or call home at a set time, and maybe find out that Irfan misses home too.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when he whispered "You awake?"
qa.a: Irfan might have been lonely or homesick himself, reaching out in the dark.

grounding: A teen at a residential school lies awake missing home food, sounds and routines, and hides it from his roommate.

passage:
Ritu Didi,
Three weeks at the new residential school, and in the daytime I'm fine. Classes are good. But at night I can't sleep. I keep thinking of Ma's mustard fish on Sundays, the conch at dusk from the Dutta house, and Baba reading the newspaper out loud even when nobody's listening. Here dinner is rajma every day, and it's so quiet I can hear the clock.
Last night I cried under the blanket. When Shalini in the next bed asked, I said I had a cold. I don't want the others to think I'm a baby. Everyone else seems fine.
Today I told Mrs Sen, our house mother. She said lots of new girls feel this, and she gave me an extra phone slot to call Ma tonight.
Can you call me on Sunday too? Just talk about home stuff.
Kalyani

qa.q: What does Kalyani hear at night in the hostel?
qa.a: It is so quiet she can hear the clock.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani tell Shalini she had a cold?
qa.a: She was afraid of seeming childish, since everyone else seemed fine.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kalyani most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mrs Sen the same day; she reassured Kalyani and arranged an extra call home.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She might feel a pang of missing her sister, and glad that Kalyani told Mrs Sen and asked for a Sunday call.

grounding: A teen at a residential school misses home food, sounds and routines at night and hides it from roommates.
